planting.note: Plant divisions in a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss; keep the pot sitting in a tray of rain water or distilled water at all times. Never use fertilized potting mix or tap water.

directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Forked sundew is named for its distinctive leaves, which repeatedly fork into two or more thin, sticky-tipped arms rather than the simple spoon or thread shape of most other sundew species, giving each leaf a branching, antler-like appearance covered in glistening, insect-trapping mucilage droplets. Small insects land on the sticky glandular hairs, triggering the leaf to slowly curl around the prey for digestion. It tolerates cooler winters better than many sundews and can go dormant, dying back to a resting bud, in cold weather before resprouting in spring. Provide full sun for the reddest coloring and most active glandular secretion.

Alice Sundew forms a neat, symmetrical rosette of wedge-shaped leaves densely covered in red, glistening, sticky glandular hairs that trap and slowly digest small insects, one of the easiest and most reliably attractive rosette-forming South African sundew species for beginners. Bright pink flowers rise on a tall stalk well above the trap rosette, opening in sequence over several days. Unlike temperate sundews it does not require a cold winter dormancy, growing steadily year-round as long as it stays warm and consistently wet, making it a good windowsill or terrarium subject in zone 9 and warmer without special winter care.

Spoon-Leaved Sundew is one of the most widely distributed and easiest sundew species to grow, forming a small, tidy rosette of spoon-shaped leaves edged in red, sticky, glistening glandular hairs that catch and digest gnats and other small insects. Small pink to white flowers appear on thin stalks above the rosette through much of the growing season. It grows continuously without a cold dormancy requirement, tolerating a wide range of humidity and light conditions better than many other sundew species, which makes it a good choice for beginners or for open terrariums. Provide full sun for the reddest leaf color and most vigorous growth.

Lance-Leaved Sundew is an Australian rainforest species with long, narrow, strap-like leaves covered in sticky red glandular hairs, notably more shade-tolerant than most other sundew species since it naturally grows in the dappled light of forest understories rather than open, sunny bogs. It spreads readily by root cuttings and by producing offshoots from the base, quickly forming a colony in a shared pot or terrarium. Because it tolerates lower light, it is a good choice for a terrarium or indoor grow-light setup where full sun is not available; give it consistently moist, wet growing medium at all times.

planting.note: Plant divisions in a well-drained mineral mix of perlite, sand, and a small amount of peat; unlike bog-type carnivorous plants, Mexican butterwort wants the soil to dry slightly between thorough waterings, especially during its winter succulent-leaved resting phase.

directions: Grow in a well-drained, mineral succulent-style mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, watering thoroughly but allowing the mix to dry slightly between waterings rather than keeping it constantly saturated like a bog plant. Mexican butterwort forms a flat rosette of broad, pale green to pink-tinged leaves coated in a glistening, sticky film that traps small gnats and fungus flies, which the leaf slowly digests, and it produces showy, large, single flowers in shades of purple, pink, or white on thin stalks well above the foliage. In winter it forms a smaller, tighter rosette of thick, non-carnivorous succulent leaves and needs less water during this resting phase, resuming its sticky carnivorous leaves as growth picks up in spring. Unlike many carnivorous plants it tolerates tap water reasonably well due to its Mexican highland origin in mineral-rich soils.
